name: Queueing Theory and Little's Law
intent: Use a little queueing mathematics to predict why latency explodes near full utilisation and to size pools, threads and servers before an outage does it for you.
scenario: A service handles 1,000 requests per second and each takes 50 ms on average. How many requests are in flight, how many workers does it need, and why does a traffic bump from 90% to 99% busy turn 50 ms responses into 5 second ones?
problem: Teams size systems by average load and are then surprised that a modest traffic increase makes latency jump by 10x or 100x, timeouts fire, clients retry, and the retries add load. The behaviour is not a bug in any one component. It is arithmetic: any resource with random arrivals and a queue has a latency curve that is flat at low utilisation and nearly vertical close to 100%, and variability makes it bend earlier.

howItWorks.title: Little's law: L = lambda x W
howItWorks.text: For any stable system, the average number of items inside it (L) equals the average arrival rate (lambda) times the average time each item spends inside (W). It needs no assumption about arrival or service distributions. At 1,000 requests per second and 50 ms, L = 1,000 x 0.05 = 50 requests in flight on average. Apply it to anything: a thread pool, a connection pool, a queue, a whole service. It also works on the queue alone (waiting items = arrival rate x mean wait).

howItWorks.title: Utilisation sets the shape of the latency curve
howItWorks.text: Utilisation is rho = lambda / (servers x service rate), the fraction of capacity in use. For one server with random (Poisson: independent, randomly spaced) arrivals and exponential service times (M/M/1, the simplest queue model), the mean time in the system is S / (1 - rho) where S is the service time, so the mean wait is S x rho / (1 - rho). At 50% busy the response time is 2x the service time, at 90% it is 10x, at 99% it is 100x. Doubling the load from 45% to 90% does not double latency, it multiplies it by 10 / 1.8, about 5.5x. Beyond 100% there is no steady state: the queue grows for as long as the overload lasts.

howItWorks.title: Variability bends the curve earlier (Kingman)
howItWorks.text: The knee is the point where the latency curve bends sharply upward. Kingman's approximation for one server says the mean wait is about (rho / (1 - rho)) x ((ca^2 + cs^2) / 2) x S, where ca and cs are the coefficients of variation (standard deviation / mean) of inter-arrival and service times. Exponential service has cs = 1. Perfectly regular service (cs = 0) halves the wait. Heavy-tailed service (cs = 3, a few slow requests among many fast ones) multiplies it by 5. Real request latencies are often heavy-tailed, so real knees arrive earlier than the textbook M/M/1 curve.

howItWorks.title: Pooling: one shared queue beats separate queues
howItWorks.text: With c servers fed from one queue (M/M/c), a request waits only when all c servers are busy, and the probability of that is given by the Erlang C formula. The knee moves to the right as c grows: 64 workers on one queue can run at 78% busy and still show a mean wait of about 0.1 ms on 50 ms work. The same 64 workers each with a private queue behave like 64 separate M/M/1 systems, and a request can wait behind a long job while another worker is idle. This is why one shared queue (or a work-stealing scheduler) beats sharding requests to workers up front. The catch: pooling does not remove the knee, it only moves it, and a bigger pool means a bigger cliff when something shared (a database) saturates.

howItWorks.title: Size pools with Little's law, then add headroom
howItWorks.text: Concurrency needed = throughput x latency. 1,000 requests per second at 50 ms needs 50 requests in flight; a pool of exactly 50 is 100% busy and unstable. Pick a target utilisation (60 to 80% is common, lower for spiky traffic or heavy-tailed service) and divide: 50 / 0.7 = 72 workers. Use the p99 service time, not the mean, when you want to cover bad moments. The same arithmetic converts a concurrency limit into a throughput ceiling: a pool of 20 connections with 40 ms queries tops out at 20 / 0.040 = 500 queries per second.

howItWorks.title: Near saturation, small changes and retries compound
howItWorks.text: Because the curve is almost vertical, a 10% rise in load at 90% busy pushes the system to 99% and latency from 10x to 100x. Clients time out, retry, and each retry is extra arrival rate: a 10% retry rate takes 90% busy to 99% busy, which causes more timeouts. Defences all work on the arrival side or the queue: bounded queues that reject early, load shedding, retries with backoff and budgets, and autoscaling that adds capacity before the knee.

pros: Back-of-the-envelope numbers (in flight, pool size, headroom) that match what production systems do
Little's law holds for any stable system whatever the distributions, so it is a safe sanity check on your own metrics
Explains hockey-stick latency, so the 70 to 80% utilisation guideline stops being folklore
Shows where more capacity pays off (before the knee) and where it does not (variability, a shared bottleneck)
cons: Closed-form results assume Poisson arrivals and steady state; real traffic is bursty, diurnal and correlated, which makes real queues worse
Needs the right definition of the system boundary and server: a pool, a CPU, a database and a lock each queue differently
Averages hide tails; the mean can look fine while p99 (the time the slowest 1% of requests take) is 10x or more worse
Closed systems (a fixed number of users who wait for replies) behave differently from open ones, and the textbook formulas are for the open case
whenToUse: Sizing thread pools, connection pools, worker fleets and concurrency limits
Deciding how much headroom a service needs before autoscaling or load shedding must kick in
Explaining or predicting a latency cliff during a capacity review or an incident
Choosing between one shared queue and per-worker queues or sharding
whenNotToUse: As a precise predictor of production latency: use it for shape and order of magnitude, then load test
For systems with strongly bursty or self-similar traffic without measuring the real arrival variability first
When the bottleneck is not a queue at all (a fixed network round trip or a cold cache dominates)
pitfalls: Sizing for average load: at 100% average utilisation the queue is unstable, and even 90% gives a 10x response time
Treating 70 to 80% as a target to hit instead of a ceiling; the right number is lower for spiky or heavy-tailed workloads
Mixing units in Little's law (requests per second x milliseconds), or applying it with arrival rate and time measured over different windows or to different boundaries
Counting only successful requests in lambda or W; failures and timeouts occupy the system too
Splitting one pool into many small ones (per tenant, per endpoint, per worker) and losing the pooling benefit without isolating failures on purpose
Adding retries without a budget: a client timeout shorter than the queueing delay turns every slow response into extra load
Using the mean service time for heavy-tailed work; a few 2 second requests among 20 ms ones can dominate the wait

roles.label: Clients
roles.description: Send requests at some average rate lambda, randomly spaced.

roles.label: Queue
roles.description: Holds requests that arrived while every worker was busy. Its length is the hockey stick.

roles.label: Worker pool
roles.description: Threads, connections or servers that serve one request each at a time.

quiz.question: An image-resize service receives 400 requests per second, and each request holds a worker for 100 ms on average. You want the pool to run at no more than 80% busy on average. What is the smallest pool that meets this?
quiz.explanation: Little's law gives 400 x 0.1 = 40 requests in flight on average. A pool of 40 would be 100% busy, which is unstable. Dividing by the 0.8 target gives 40 / 0.8 = 50 workers.

quiz.question: One worker serves requests with random arrivals and exponentially distributed service times averaging 20 ms. At 50% busy the mean response time is 40 ms. Traffic grows until the worker is 90% busy. What mean response time should you expect?
quiz.explanation: Mean response time is S / (1 - rho), so at 90% busy it is 20 / 0.1 = 200 ms. Load grew by 1.8x but latency grew by 5x. Scaling latency in proportion to load is the tempting mistake, because the curve is nearly vertical close to full utilisation.

quiz.question: A 16-worker service hashes each request to one worker's private queue. Every worker averages 70% busy, yet p99 is poor, and monitoring shows requests waiting while some other worker sits idle. You cannot add hardware. Which change helps most?
options: Let all 16 workers pull from one shared queue
Give each worker a larger private queue
Cut the client timeout so slow requests fail sooner
Rehash with a different function to balance keys
quiz.explanation: One shared queue means a request waits only when all 16 workers are busy, so the knee moves far to the right. Private queues behave like 16 separate M/M/1 systems, where a request can wait behind a long job next to an idle worker. A bigger private queue only stores more waiting requests, and a new hash still cannot move work to an idle worker.
